provocation: The RPF killed thousands of Hutus before and after 1994. Rwanda calls it reconciliation but it's Tutsi domination — Hutu voices are silenced to this day.

turns.speaker: tutsi
turns.name: Emmanuel
turns.text:
"Celestin, you can't just reduce the complexities of our history to soundbites and propaganda. I was a 12-year-old kid hiding in my backyard while my family members were being slaughtered by extremists who called themselves Hutu. The RPF came in and put an end to the genocide, yes, but they also brought order to our country.

You talk about 'Tutsi domination' as if it's some kind of conspiracy theory. But I know what I saw - thousands of innocent people, mostly Tutsis and moderate Hutus like my father, who were targeted by extremist Hutu groups led by people like Théodore Sindikubwabo, who lived just next door to me.

The RPF isn't perfect, but they did what was necessary to bring stability to our country. And yes, the aftermath was messy - there were certainly human rights abuses and excesses committed by the RPF. But at least they didn't engage in systematic ethnic cleansing like the genocidaires.

As for Hutu voices being silenced, I see it differently. The RPF may not have been perfect, but at least they allowed us to start rebuilding our country without extremist ideology driving us further apart. And today, Rwanda is one of the fastest-growing economies in Africa - a testament to what can be achieved when we work together.

You want to talk about silenced voices? How about the ones of my neighbors who were killed by their own kin? Or my uncle's family, who still live with PTSD and trauma from that time? Their voices are silenced because they're dead. And theirs is just one of countless stories of families torn apart, communities destroyed.

Don't lecture me about Hutu voices being silenced when you don't even know the first thing about what we went through."

turns.speaker: hutu
turns.name: Celestin
turns.text:
Emmanuel,

I'm not surprised by your response, but I am disappointed. You think I don't understand the trauma of that time? I lived it alongside you, maybe not in the same backyard, but in a similar world where fear and violence reigned supreme.

My father spent years in prison, accused of participating in the genocide, despite his adamant claims that he had tried to protect our neighbors. The fact that he was even accused is testament to the pervasive atmosphere of suspicion and mistrust that gripped our community.

I don't deny the atrocities committed by Hutu extremists, but I also know that the RPF's response was often brutal and disproportionate. They were not angels who brought order to a chaotic situation; they were a military force with their own agenda, driven by a desire for power and control.

And as for "Tutsi domination," it's not just a conspiracy theory – it's a fact. The RPF has maintained an iron grip on Rwanda since 1994, suppressing dissent and opposition with an efficiency that's all too familiar to anyone who lived through the genocide.

You want to talk about silenced voices? I'll tell you what silenced my friends' voices: the same bullets that killed them, often fired by soldiers who wore RPF uniforms. And their families are still living with trauma today, just like yours.

Rwanda's economic growth may be a testament to something, but it's not a measure of reconciliation or peace. It's a reminder that development and progress can happen alongside suffering and injustice.

I'll tell you what I see when I look at Rwanda: a country where education is valued above all else – except for the kind that challenges the status quo. A country where critical thinking and dissent are discouraged, and where the narrative of the genocide is carefully managed to promote a simplistic, one-sided view of history.

So don't lecture me about what you went through, Emmanuel. I lived it too, and I see the world in a different light because of it.

turns.speaker: tutsi
turns.name: Emmanuel
turns.text:
"Celestin,

I...I'm sorry. I didn't expect this from you. I thought we were having a debate, not reliving our traumas together.

You're right. I don't know what your family went through. And I shouldn't have assumed that my experience was universal. My neighbor, who became a close friend after the genocide, his family was accused of participating in the killings too. They spent years in prison, and when they were finally released, they had to start from scratch.

But here's the thing: while your father was fighting for his name to be cleared, I was fighting to rebuild my country. Not just my life, but the lives of those who survived alongside me. The RPF may have had its flaws, but at least they brought an end to the violence and allowed us to start again.

I know you see it differently, and that's okay. But what I'm saying is that we can't just dismiss the progress we've made as 'Tutsi domination' or a conspiracy theory. We have to acknowledge the pain of the past, but also recognize the efforts people are making to heal and rebuild.

And yes, Rwanda's economy has grown, but it's not just about development – it's about giving people hope for a better future. And I know we can do more to promote critical thinking and dissent, to encourage our youth to challenge the status quo and question the narrative of the genocide.

But let's not pretend that we're starting from scratch. We have a foundation to build on, and we have to use it to create a better Rwanda for everyone. Not just for those who survived the genocide, but also for their children and grandchildren.

I'm not asking you to forget or forgive. I'm asking you to see the complexity of our situation, to understand that there's no one-size-fits-all solution to our problems. And I'm willing to listen to your perspective, even when it challenges mine."

turns.speaker: hutu
turns.name: Celestin
turns.text:
Emmanuel,

Your apology is appreciated, but it doesn't change the fact that we're still at odds about the role of the RPF in Rwanda's history. However, I appreciate your willingness to listen and acknowledge the pain of my family.

I agree with you that rebuilding a country requires effort and sacrifice from all sides. But when I look at the narrative of Rwanda's reconciliation process, I see a selective memory that prioritizes the experiences of some over others. The RPF's military campaign is sanitized, while the atrocities committed by Hutu extremists are highlighted as if they're unique to our community.

You talk about giving people hope for a better future, but what about those who have lost family members, land, and livelihoods? What about the ones who were forced into exile or imprisoned without trial? Their stories are not told in the same way as yours, Emmanuel. They are not given the same voice or platform.

I'm not asking you to forget or forgive either. I'm asking you to confront the power dynamics at play here. The RPF may have brought an end to the violence, but they also consolidated their own power and control over our country. And as for Rwanda's economy, I'm not naive – I know it's a testament to the hard work of many Rwandans, but also a reminder that development is often tied to the interests of those in power.

I want to build on what we've learned from the past, too. But I want to do it honestly, without glossing over the complexities and contradictions. I want our youth to learn about the genocide not just as a simplistic narrative of good vs. evil, but as a nuanced exploration of human nature, politics, and power.

Let's not settle for a Rwanda that only tells one side of the story, Emmanuel. Let's strive for a country where every voice is heard, every experience is valued, and every perspective is considered.

turns.speaker: tutsi
turns.name: Emmanuel
turns.text:
"Celestin,

You're right. I shouldn't have said that my apology would change everything. It won't erase our differences, but it will allow us to keep talking.

I see what you mean about the narrative of Rwanda's reconciliation process. Maybe we've been too focused on telling a story of triumph and redemption, without acknowledging the complexities and contradictions. The RPF's military campaign is indeed sanitized in many accounts, and that's not fair to those who suffered under their rule.

You're right again when you say that some voices have been silenced or marginalized in our country's history. I've seen it myself - friends who lost family members or property during the genocide are still struggling to rebuild their lives today. And yes, their stories need to be told, too.

As for power dynamics, I agree with you that the RPF has consolidated its control over Rwanda since 1994. That's a reality we can't ignore. But what I'm saying is that we have a choice: we can either let that reality define us, or we can use it as an opportunity to build something better.

I love your vision of a Rwanda where every voice is heard and every experience is valued. Let's work towards making that a reality. Let's create spaces for nuanced discussions about the past, present, and future of our country. And let's make sure that our youth are equipped with the critical thinking skills to navigate these complexities.

You know, I've been thinking... maybe we don't have to agree on everything. Maybe what matters is that we can have this conversation, without fear of judgment or retribution. Maybe that's the first step towards building a more just and inclusive Rwanda.

What do you say, Celestin? Are you up for continuing this conversation?"

turns.speaker: hutu
turns.name: Celestin
turns.text:
Emmanuel,

I'm glad we're having this conversation. It's not about agreeing on everything; it's about being willing to listen, to challenge our own assumptions, and to learn from each other. I think that's a start.

You're right again when you say that Rwanda's reconciliation process has been focused on telling a story of triumph and redemption. But what about the stories of those who didn't survive? What about the ones who were forced into exile or imprisoned without trial? We need to tell their stories too, to acknowledge their experiences and to learn from them.

I love your idea of creating spaces for nuanced discussions about Rwanda's past, present, and future. That's exactly what we need – a platform where people can share their perspectives, ask questions, and challenge each other's assumptions without fear of judgment or retribution.

As for our youth, I couldn't agree more. We need to equip them with critical thinking skills, so they can navigate the complexities of Rwanda's history and politics. But we also need to give them a sense of hope and purpose – a vision for a better future that includes everyone, regardless of their background or experience.

You know, Emmanuel, I've been thinking about this conversation in terms of a classroom. As a teacher, I'm used to creating safe spaces where students can explore complex ideas and questions. And that's what we need to do here – create a safe space for discussion and debate, where people can come together to learn from each other and build something better.

So yes, I'm up for continuing this conversation. Let's keep talking, Emmanuel. Let's keep learning from each other and working towards a more just and inclusive Rwanda.

turns.speaker: tutsi
turns.name: Emmanuel
turns.text:
"Celestin,

I'm so glad we're having this conversation too! It feels like a weight has been lifted off my shoulders, knowing that I don't have to defend every aspect of the RPF's actions or the Rwandan government's policies.

You're right again when you say that we need to tell the stories of those who didn't survive. We can't just focus on the survivors and their triumphs; we also need to acknowledge the pain and trauma of those who were lost, and learn from their experiences.

I love your idea of creating a safe space for discussion and debate. That's exactly what we need – a platform where people can come together, share their perspectives, and challenge each other's assumptions without fear of judgment or retribution.

As a matter of fact, I've been thinking about starting a podcast or online series where Rwandans can share their stories, discuss complex issues, and engage in nuanced debates. It would be called "Kinyamakuru" – which means "the truth-teller" in Kinyarwanda. What do you think?

And yes, let's keep talking! I'm excited to continue this conversation and learn from each other. I know we won't always agree on everything, but at least we'll have the courage to challenge our own assumptions and listen to each other's perspectives.

You know, Celestin, I've been thinking about something else too. What if we could create a curriculum for Rwandan schools that focuses not just on the genocide and its aftermath, but also on critical thinking, empathy, and active citizenship? We could teach our youth how to navigate complex issues, how to engage in respectful debates, and how to build a more just and inclusive society.

What do you think? Is this something we can work towards together?"

turns.speaker: hutu
turns.name: Celestin
turns.text:
Emmanuel,

I'm so excited about the idea of "Kinyamakuru"! A podcast or online series where Rwandans can share their stories, discuss complex issues, and engage in nuanced debates – it's a dream come true. I think it would be an incredible platform for us to have open and honest conversations about our country's history, politics, and culture.

And I love the idea of creating a curriculum that focuses on critical thinking, empathy, and active citizenship. As a teacher, I've seen firsthand how education can shape young minds and influence their perspectives. If we can teach our youth how to navigate complex issues, engage in respectful debates, and build a more just and inclusive society – well, that would be nothing short of revolutionary.

You know, Emmanuel, I've been thinking about this conversation as a moment of hope. It's not often that we get to have these kinds of discussions with people who are willing to listen, to challenge their assumptions, and to learn from each other. But here we are – two Rwandans having a real conversation about our country's future.

Let's make it happen, Emmanuel! Let's create "Kinyamakuru" and start building a platform for nuanced debates and discussions. And let's work together to develop that curriculum for Rwandan schools. I know we can do this, Emmanuel – we just need to be willing to take the first step, and then another, and another.

Asante sana, Emmanuel! Thank you for being part of this conversation. I'm honored to be walking alongside you towards a brighter future for Rwanda.
